opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the clearest way to frame it is that the two markets reward different things, so the same technology turns into quite different businesses.

In the US, the biggest opportunity is enterprise software. American companies are used to paying for SaaS, for subscriptions, for tools that save employee time. Labor is expensive, so if an AI product can replace or augment even part of a knowledgeable worker's job, say a paralegal, a support agent, or a junior engineer, the ROI is obvious and a company will pay real money per seat or per task. That's why you see so many US AI startups going vertical: legal, healthcare, coding, finance. The model layer is dominated by a few very well-capitalized labs, and the application layer sits on top with healthy margins because customers will pay for value.

China is different in a few ways. First, willingness to pay for software in the enterprise is historically lower. Many companies prefer to build in-house or expect heavy customization, so pure SaaS has always been hard there. Second, labor costs, while rising, are still lower, so "we replace a person" is a weaker pitch. Third, the consumer internet in China is extremely mature and competitive. The super apps already own the user's time, so a lot of AI value gets captured by the big platforms, like ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent, which integrate AI into products people already use rather than letting a new standalone app break through.

So in China, the winning models tend to look like this: AI embedded into high-traffic consumer products and monetized through ads, e-commerce, or games rather than subscriptions; price competition at the model layer, where you saw API prices crash toward almost zero very quickly, which pushes model companies to find revenue elsewhere; and going overseas. A lot of Chinese AI entrepreneurs build apps for global users from day one, because they can combine strong engineering and fast iteration with a market where users actually pay, photo and video tools, companion apps, productivity apps.

There's also a hardware and manufacturing angle in China that's underrated. The supply chain is right there, so AI plus devices, robotics, and industrial applications are areas where Chinese teams have a natural advantage.

If I simplify it: in the US, AI is largely a story about selling productivity to businesses at high prices. In China, it's more a story about scale, distribution, and efficiency, either inside big platforms, in the physical world, or by exporting products to global consumers. Neither is better; founders just need to be honest about which game they're playing.

r001.rationale: The response describes U.S. enterprise software and vertical AI startups, but does not connect specialized model providers to a broader culture of division of labor across industries.

r002.rationale: It says U.S. customers pay for value and application companies can have healthy margins, but does not explain that revenue potential across the value chain lets companies leave opportunities for other ecosystem participants.

r003.rationale: The response mentions lower enterprise software willingness to pay and AI embedded in major platforms, but does not link end users’ limited ability to pay to Chinese companies offering integrated, end-to-end solutions.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I get asked a lot, and I think the honest answer is that the two markets are solving the same technology problem under completely different economic constraints.

In the United States, the dominant business model is still the one Silicon Valley has run for twenty years: raise a lot of capital, build the best model or the best product, charge enterprises and developers for it, and let the cloud layer absorb the cost. The customers are there. American companies have been paying for software for decades, so a CIO will sign a seven-figure contract for an AI tool if it saves headcount or speeds up engineering. That willingness to pay is what lets the frontier labs justify spending billions on compute. The flywheel is capital, then capability, then enterprise revenue, then more capital.

China is different in three ways. First, the cost of compute is structurally higher because of export controls, so you can't just brute-force your way to the frontier. That has pushed Chinese labs toward efficiency as a core competency: distillation, mixture of experts, cheaper training recipes. Some of the most interesting algorithmic work is coming out of China precisely because the constraint forced it.

Second, software has historically been hard to monetize there. Enterprise customers expect a lot of customization for very little money, and consumers have been trained for fifteen years that apps are free. So the pure API business, where you sell tokens to developers, is a much weaker model in China. The big players have responded by driving prices down aggressively, almost to zero, and treating the model as a traffic acquisition cost rather than a product.

Third, and this is the part people in the US often miss, China's advantage is in deployment, not in the model itself. You have a manufacturing base, a huge services economy, logistics, hardware. The valuable question in China isn't "who has the best model," it's "who can put a model inside a factory, a car, a delivery network, or a short-video app and make it change the unit economics." That's why so much of the energy there is going into applications, consumer products, and embodied AI rather than into foundation model races.

So if I had to compress it: American AI companies make money by selling intelligence. Chinese AI companies, for the most part, will make money by embedding intelligence into things people already pay for. Neither is obviously superior. The US model concentrates value in a handful of labs and cloud providers. The Chinese model spreads it thinner but reaches physical industries much faster.

The thing I'd watch is open source. When Chinese labs release strong open models, it undercuts the premium American labs can charge, and that pressure crosses the Pacific whether anyone likes it or not.

r001.rationale: The response describes U.S. firms selling models and products to enterprises and developers, but does not connect that opportunity to a broader culture of division of labor across industries.

r002.rationale: It says U.S. enterprise revenue helps frontier labs fund further development, but does not explain that revenue potential across the value chain leaves opportunities for other ecosystem participants.

r003.rationale: It notes Chinese customers’ limited willingness to pay and emphasizes deployment into existing products and industries, but does not clearly say this leads companies to offer integrated, end-to-end offerings.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to separate the opportunity in the technology from the opportunity to build a business around it. The technology may be similar, but who pays, what they pay for, and how you reach them can be quite different.

In the United States, companies have an established habit of paying for software, and labor is expensive. So if an AI product helps an engineer, a lawyer, or a sales team do more work, there can be a straightforward business case. That supports subscriptions, usage-based pricing, and products sold directly to businesses. There is also an opportunity to build the underlying models and sell access to other developers, although that requires substantial capital.

In China, I would look more closely at distribution and integration into an existing business. Consumers may use a product heavily without being willing to pay a separate subscription, while enterprise customers may want a complete solution rather than another software tool. So the business model might involve implementation and services, or monetization through commerce, advertising, and transactions. The challenge is to make those solutions repeatable, so every new customer doesn’t become a separate consulting project.

Those are tendencies, not absolute rules. A Chinese company can build a subscription product for global customers, and an American company can struggle to get anyone to pay. Ultimately, I’d ask the same questions in both markets: Whose problem are you solving? How much value do you create? And can you capture enough of that value to cover the cost of delivering it? A large number of users is an opportunity, but it isn’t yet a business model.

r001.rationale: The response mentions selling model access to developers, but does not connect specialized model providers to a broader U.S. culture of division of labor across industries.

r002.rationale: It says companies can sell software or model access, but does not explain that revenue potential across the value chain lets firms leave opportunities for other ecosystem participants.

r003.rationale: It says Chinese consumers may not pay a separate subscription and that enterprise customers may prefer complete solutions, but does not clearly link consumers’ limited ability to pay to companies’ emphasis on integrated, end-to-end offerings.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d look at three things: who pays, what problem they’re paying to solve, and how you reach them.

In the United States, companies often have more room to sell AI as software. If a product saves an employee several hours a week, there can be a clear budget for it. That supports subscriptions, usage-based pricing, and specialized tools for particular professions. There’s also an opportunity to build a platform that other developers use, although that requires substantial capital and a strong technical advantage.

In China, I think the opportunity often depends more on connecting AI to an existing business process. Customers may be less willing to pay for a standalone AI assistant, but they’ll pay for better customer service, more effective sales, or lower operating costs. So the business model may involve implementation, integration, and ongoing service, with AI embedded inside the solution.

Of course, that’s a difference in emphasis, not a hard boundary. American customers also need integration, and Chinese customers also buy software. The practical question for a founder is: can you deliver a measurable result, and can you deliver it repeatedly without turning every customer into a separate consulting project?

That’s where I’d focus. A popular model or a lot of users doesn’t automatically make a business. You need a customer who gets enough value to keep paying, and a cost structure that leaves you a margin.

r001.rationale: It mentions specialized tools for particular professions, but does not connect that opportunity to a broader U.S. culture of division of labor across industries.

r002.rationale: It discusses subscriptions, usage-based pricing, and platform opportunities, but does not explain that high potential revenue across the U.S. value chain leaves opportunities for other ecosystem participants.

r003.rationale: It says Chinese customers may be less willing to pay for standalone assistants and describes implementation, integration, and embedded AI. It does not state that limited capacity to pay drives this model or clearly describe end-to-end offerings.
